verses.zh: 但愿你们宽容我这一点愚妄，其实你们原是宽容我的。
verses.en: I wish that you would be patient with me in a little foolishness, but indeed you are being patient with me!
verses.commentary:
11:1 "I wish that you would bear with me" This is an IMPERFECT MIDDLE INDICATIVE.
The MIDDLE VOICE matches the emphatic personal introduction to chapter 10. The
IMPERFECT TENSE can mean

- repeated action in past time

- the beginning of an action

Number two fits this context best.

See fuller note on "bear" at 2 Cor. 11:4.

▣ "in a little foolishness" Paul has previously stated that physical comparison
is foolishness, but the false teachers had used him as the object of ridicule. Therefore,
he uses the Sophist's rhetorical style (i.e., boasting) against them (i.e., a sarcastic parody).
He had to defend himself before this church for their own good. He felt silly in having to do
this as verses 17 and 21 affirm.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SOPHISTS

▣ "indeed you are bearing with me" This is either a PRESENT MIDDLE INDICATIVE
(NASB, NKJV, NJB) or a PRESENT MIDDLE IMPERATIVE (NRSV, TEV).

There are three reasons stated in 2 Cor. 11:2, 4, 5 why they should listen. Each of these reasons
is introduced in English by the word "for" (gar).

verses.zh: 我为你们起的愤恨，原是　神那样的愤恨。因为我曾把你们许配一个丈夫，要把你们如同贞洁的童女，献给基督。
verses.en: For I am jealous for you with godly jealousy, because I promised you in marriage to one husband,[NOTE:1] to present you as a pure[NOTE:2] virgin to Christ.
notes: That is, to Christ.
Or “chaste.”
verses.commentary:
11:2 "I betrothed you to one husband, so that to Christ" Paul, as the founder of this
church, is acting like a parent to betroth them to Christ (cf. Eph. 5:22-33; Rev. 19:9; 21:2,9;
22:17). This follows OT imagery of God as husband (cf. Isa. 54:5; 62:5; Jer. 3:14; 31:32; Hosea 2:19).

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANTHROPOMORPHIC LANGUAGE TO DESCRIBE GOD

▣ "I might present you as a pure virgin" This is the OT terminology for a
marriage ceremony. Paul repeats this same theme in Eph. 5:25-27. Paul is subtly rebuking the
Corinthian Christians for even listening to the itinerant false teachers. In a sense those believers
or house churches who supported these false teachers had become spiritually unfaithful
(i.e., OT spiritual adultery).

verses.zh: 我只怕你们的心或偏于邪，失去那向基督所存纯一清洁的心，就像蛇用诡诈诱惑了夏娃一样。
verses.en: But I am afraid that[NOTE:1] just as the serpent[NOTE:2] deceived Eve by his treachery,[NOTE:3] your minds may be led astray[NOTE:4] from a sincere and pure[NOTE:5] devotion to Christ.
notes: Grk “I fear lest somehow.”
Or “the snake.”
Or “craftiness.”
Or “corrupted,” “seduced.”

Although most mss (א2 H Ψ 0121 0243 1739 1881 M) lack “and pure” (καὶ τῆς ἁγνότητος, kai tēs hagnotētos; Grk “and purity”) several significant and early witnesses (P46 א* B D[2] F G 33 81 104 ar r co) retain these words. Their presence in such mss across such a wide geographical distribution argues for their authenticity. The omission from the majority of mss can be explained by haplography, since the -τητος ending of ἁγνότητος is identical to the ending of ἁπλότητος (haplotētos, “sincerity”) three words back (ἁπλότητος καὶ τῆς ἁγνότητος); further, since the meanings of “sincerity” and “purity” are similar they might seem redundant. A copyist would scarcely notice the omission because Paul’s statement still makes sense without “and from purity.”
verses.commentary:
11:3 "as the serpent deceived Eve by his craftiness" This refers to the temptation account
found in Genesis 3 (cf. 1 Tim. 2:14). Remember the serpent led Eve away from YHWH in small steps
leading to self-assertive independence!

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE SERPENT

▣ "deceived" The term deceived (exapataō) is used only by Paul in the NT
(cf. Rom. 7:11; 16:18; 1 Cor. 3:18; 2 Cor. 11:3; 2 Thess. 2:3; 1 Tim. 2:14). The unintensified
form, apataō, is used in the Septuagint of Gen. 3:13 of Eve. Paul uses it in Eph. 5:6
and 1 Tim. 2:14 (twice). Deception comes both from without and within. Believers must be
constantly on guard.

▣ "craftiness" The term craftiness (panourgia) is a compound from "all" (pan) and
"work" (ergon). Paul has used it twice before in his Corinthian letters (cf. 1 Cor. 3:19;
2 Cor. 4:2). Paul understood the spiritual warfare which believers had to face (cf. 2:2; Eph. 4:14). He
states the results of evil on mankind clearly in Romans 1-3 and on believers in Romans 7; Eph. 6:10-19.
Paul's theology begins with angelic and human rebellion.

SPECIAL TOPIC: WAR IN HEAVEN

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND

SPECIAL TOPIC: SCHEMES

▣ "your minds will be led astray" The VERB phtheirō is
an AORIST PASSIVE SUBJUNCTIVE. In a further allusion to Genesis 3 Paul used this term
for "ruin" or "spoil" in a moral sense several times (cf. 2 Cor. 7:2; 11:3; 1 Cor. 3:17; 15:33;
Eph. 4:22). Believers can be tricked, manipulated, and defeated by evil!

▣ "from the simplicity" See note at 2 Cor. 1:12.

▣ "and purity" There is a Greek manuscript variant which adds "and purity." It is found
in MSS P46, א*, B, and G (cf. NASB, NRSV,
TEV, NIV). It is absent in MSS אc, Dc, H, K,
and P (cf. Peshitta, NKJV, NJB, REB). The MS D* has the longer reading also, but the terms are
in reverse order. Textual scholars are split on which is original. The inclusion of "purity" picks
up on 2 Cor. 11:2 and is included in some very good and geographically diverse ancient manuscripts. The
translation committee of the UBS4 could not decide which option they thought was original.

NASB
"of devotion to Christ"

NKJV, Peshitta
"that is in Christ"

NRSV, TEV, NJB, NIV
"devotion to Christ"

REB
"simple-hearted devotion to Christ"

Peshitta
"the sincerity that is in Christ"

The ABLATIVE PREPOSITION, apo, introduces three
OBJECTS.

- from simplicity

- from purity

- from "to Christ"

What is the referent in 2 Cor. 11:3? Several English translations supply "devotion," but
it could refer to "in Christ," which is Paul's famous phrase of personal faith in Christ.

verses.zh: 假如有人来另传一个耶稣，不是我们所传过的；或者你们另受一个灵，不是你们所受过的；或者另得一个福音，不是你们所得过的；你们容让他也就罢了。
verses.en: For if someone comes and proclaims[NOTE:1] another Jesus different from the one we proclaimed,[NOTE:2] or if you receive a different spirit than the one you received,[NOTE:3] or a different gospel than the one you accepted,[NOTE:4] you put up with it well enough![NOTE:5]
notes: Or “preaches.”
Grk “another Jesus whom we have not proclaimed.”
Grk “a different spirit which you did not receive.”
Grk “a different gospel which you did not accept.”
Or “you endure it very well.”
verses.commentary:
11:4 "For if one comes" This a FIRST CLASS CONDITIONAL SENTENCE which is
assumed to be true from the author's perspective or for his literary purpose. "One" seems to refer
to the chief false teacher alluded to in 2 Cor. 10:7,10.

▣ "another Jesus whom we have not preached" These false teachers were not disagreeing
over some peripheral, minor matter, but over the person and work of Jesus Christ (cf. 1 Cor. 3:11). It
is obvious in putting all the evidence together that these false teachers were a mixture of both the
Judaizers as in the book of Galatians and the Hellenists (i.e., Sophists). These surrogates
from Jerusalem had dropped the circumcision emphasis, probably because of the Jerusalem Council's
findings in Acts 15, but they continued their Jewish legalism somehow combined with or refined by
Hellenistic (i.e., Sophists) thinking.

It is possible that Paul is using the false teachers' charges against him. They may
have accused him of "preaching another gospel."

Those of us who believe the Bible is the inspired word of God have several
questions to answer.

- Do we read the NT through the eyes of the OT or does the NT have interpretive preeminence?

- Are the words of Paul (or any NT author) as inspired as the words of Jesus?

- Does the presence of "some" diversity among NT authors allow modern interpreters some
"wiggle room" on some issues? Do we allow this same thing among the early church interpreters
(i.e., Greek and Latin Church Fathers; later church leaders [Augustine, Aquinas, Luther,
Calvin, etc.])? Or to put it another way, how does one understand (define, limit) orthodoxy?

SPECIAL TOPIC: ORTHODOXY OF THE PASTORALS

▣ "or you receive a different spirit which you have not received" Some see this as a
reference to the Holy Spirit (cf. Gal. 4:6; TEV), but it seems preferable to relate this to either

- the "spirit of fear and slavery" (cf. Rom. 8:15; 2 Tim. 1:7)

- "the spirit of peace and joy" (cf. Rom. 14:17)

- for a fuller note on "spirit" see 1 Cor. 2:11

The term "different" is heteros, which means another of a different kind.
Paul is contrasting the messages of the false teachers and himself (cf. Gal. 1:6). There is much
similarity between the problems mentioned in Gal.1:6-9 and here.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SPIRIT IN THE NT

▣ "received. . .accepted" The Greek verbs lambanō and dechomai are
synonymous. Both basic meanings are to take hold of something. The two notes in Louw and Nida's
Greek-English Lexicon, vol. 1, are helpful.

- "to receive or accept an object or benefit for which the initiative rests with the giver,
but the focus of attention in the transfer is upon the receiver" (p. 572)

- footnote 31, "There may be some subtle distinction in meaning between dechomai
and lambanō with the latter implying more active participation on the part
of the one who receives the gift, but this cannot be determined from existing contexts" (p. 572).

For me as an evangelical Christian, these terms are crucial in an appropriate response t
o the gospel (cf. John 1:12-3:16). The promises of God, the works of Christ, and the wooing of the Spirit
must be responded to both initially and continually. This forms the basis of the covenant concept
(i.e., God initiates, but humans must respond).

Lambanō is recurrent in this context (cf. 2 Cor. 11:4,8,20,24; 12:16).

SPECIAL TOPIC: RECEIVE

SPECIAL TOPIC: WHAT DOES IT MEAN TO "RECEIVE," "BELIEVE," "CONFESS/PROFESS," AND "CALL UPON"?

NASB
"you bear this beautifully"

NKJV
"you may well put up with it"

NRSV
"you submit to it readily enough"

TEV
"you gladly tolerate"

NJB
"and you put up with that only too willingly"

REB
"you put up with that well enough"

Peshitta
"you might have listened to him"

This is either a PRESENT MIDDLE IMPERATIVE or a PRESENT
MIDDLE INDICATIVE. This is biting sarcasm directed at the Corinthian Christians' willingness
to listen to these false teachers.

Paul uses this term, anechomai, several times in this chapter (cf. 2 Cor. 11:1,4,10,20).

- In 2 Cor. 11:1 it is used in the sense of "endure" (cf. 1 Cor. 4:12).

- In 2 Cor. 11:4,19,20 it is used sarcastically in the sense of "tolerate."

verses.zh: 但我想，我一点不在那些最大的使徒以下。
verses.en: For I consider myself not at all inferior to those “super-apostles.”[NOTE:1]
notes: The implicit irony in Paul’s remark is brought out well by the TEV “I do not think that I am the least bit inferior to those very special so-called ‘apostles’ of yours!”sn The ‘super-apostles’ refers either (1) to the original apostles (the older interpretation) or (2) more probably, to Paul’s opponents in Corinth, in which case the designation is ironic.
verses.commentary:
11:5 "For I consider" In this literary unit Paul uses this VERB, logizomai,
often (cf. 2 Cor. 10:2,7,11; 11:5; 12:6). It may have been a catch-word or often-used term of the
Sophist's false teachers.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CONSIDER

▣ "not in the least inferior" The VERB in this phrase is a PERFECT
ACTIVE INFINITIVE. At no time, past or present, did Paul think of himself as less than
these supposed authoritative representatives from Jerusalem (cf. 2 Cor. 12:11). This perspective is also
discussed in Gal. 1:11-2:14, where Paul also defends his apostleship.

NASB, NKJV
"to the most eminent apostles"

NRSV
"to these super-apostles"

TEV
"to these very special so-called apostles of yours"

NJB, REB
"to the super-apostles"

Peshitta
"to the most distinguished apostles"

This sarcastic description is a combination of two Greek terms, huper
(i.e., over and above) and lian (i.e., great or exceedingly). This descriptive phrase is
rare and Paul uses it only here and in 2 Cor. 12:11. Verse 5 is contextually and grammatically
linked to 2 Cor. 11:4, which obviously refers to the false teachers (cf. 2 Cor. 11:13-15). Paul
is using the term "apostles" sarcastically in its two senses:

- the Twelve

- messengers sent from churches (cf. 2 Cor. 11:13)

Apparently these false teachers had some connection with the church in Jerusalem
(cf. 2 Cor. 11:22 shows by inference that they claimed

- a Jewish background

- 12:1 shows that they claimed charismatic experiences

SPECIAL TOPIC: APOSTLES (send)

▣ "most eminent" (huperlian) See

SPECIAL TOPIC: PAUL'S USE OF HUPER COMPOUNDS

verses.zh: 我的言语虽然粗俗，我的知识却不粗俗。这是我们在凡事上向你们众人显明出来的。
verses.en: And even if I am unskilled[NOTE:1] in speaking, yet I am certainly not so in knowledge. Indeed, we have made this plain to you in everything in every way.
notes: Unskilled in speaking means not professionally trained as a rhetorician.
verses.commentary:
11:6 "But even if" This is a FIRST CLASS CONDITIONAL SENTENCE. Paul admitted
to them that Greek rhetoric was not his strength. His strength was the inspired content of his
messages.

▣ "I am unskilled in speech" This term is used in the sense of "untrained" or "amateurish"

- in Acts 4:13, where it is used of Peter and John

- in 1 Corinthians 14, where it is used of those who are unlearned in spiritual gifts

- related to Paul's confession that he was not skilled in rhetoric (cf. 2 Cor. 10:10; 1 Cor. 1:17)

This comment, apparently from the false teachers, shows that they honored rhetorical
speaking. This implies a Hellenistic (i.e., Sophists) background. See Bruce W. Winter, Philo and
Paul Among the Sophists.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SOPHISTS

verses.zh: 我因为白白传　神的福音给你们，就自居卑微，叫你们高升，这算是我犯罪吗？
verses.en: Or did I commit a sin by humbling myself[NOTE:1] so that you could be exalted, because I proclaimed[NOTE:2] the gospel of God to you free of charge?
notes: Paul is referring to humbling himself to the point of doing manual labor to support himself.
Or “preached.”
verses.commentary:
11:7 "did I commit a sin in humbling myself so that you might be exalted" Verse 7 is a question
which expects a "no" answer. This is another example of Paul's sarcasm related to the continuing
controversy of his not accepting monetary remuneration from the Corinthian church (cf. 1 Cor. 9:3-18).

The word "sin" (hamartia) is used in a non-moral sense of "did I make a mistake"
or "misjudgment." Remember, context, context, context - determines word meaning. Be careful of pre-set
theological definitions of words read into every occurrence!

▣ "the gospel of God" Notice the gospel of Christ (cf. 2 Cor. 2:12; 9:13; 10:14) is also
the gospel of God, not of Paul!

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE GOSPEL

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE KERYGMA OF THE EARLY CHURCH

verses.zh: 我亏负了别的教会，向他们取了工价来给你们效力。
verses.en: I robbed other churches by receiving support from them so that I could serve you![NOTE:1]
notes: That is, serve them free of charge (cf. the end of v. 7).
verses.commentary:
11:8 "I robbed other churches" The Greeks and Romans were used to paying their itinerant
teachers, but Paul knew that this would be the source of criticism by the false teachers and he
refused to accept monetary help from this church (or any other church while he worked among them,
cf. 1 Thess. 2:5-9; 2 Thess. 3:7-9). Paul did accept help from both Philippi and Thessalonica after
he had left (cf. Phil. 4:15-18 and possibly 1 Thess. 3:6). Apparently it hurt this church's feelings
(cf. 2 Cor. 11:11; 12:13,14; 1 Cor. 9:12,15,18).

▣ "churches" See

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHURCH (ekklēsia)

▣ "to serve you" See

SPECIAL TOPIC: SERVANT LEADERSHIP

verses.zh: 我在你们那里缺乏的时候，并没有累着你们一个人；因我所缺乏的，那从马其顿来的弟兄们都补足了。我向来凡事谨守，后来也必谨守，总不至于累着你们。
verses.en: When[NOTE:1] I was with you and was in need, I was not a burden to anyone, for the brothers who came from Macedonia fully supplied my needs.[NOTE:2] I[NOTE:3] kept myself from being a burden to you in any way, and will continue to do so.
notes: Grk “you, and when.” A new sentence was started here in the translation.

If the participle ἐλθόντες (elthontes) is taken as temporal rather than adjectival, the translation would be, “for the brothers, when they came from Macedonia, fully supplied my needs” (similar to NASB).
Grk “needs, and I kept.” A new sentence was started here in the translation.

verses.zh: 既有基督的诚实在我里面，就无人能在亚该亚一带地方阻挡我这自夸。
verses.en: As the truth of Christ is in me, this boasting of mine[NOTE:1] will not be stopped[NOTE:2] in the regions of Achaia.
notes: That is, that Paul offers the gospel free of charge to the Corinthians (see 2 Cor 11:7).
Or “silenced.”
verses.commentary:
11:10 "As the truth of Christ is in me" This is an idiomatic way of asserting

- truthfulness

- Paul's sense of inspiration (see full note at 2 Cor. 1:23)

SPECIAL TOPIC: "TRUTH" IN PAUL'S WRITINGS

SPECIAL TOPIC: INSPIRATION

▣ "this boasting of mine will not be stopped in the regions of Achaia" This is a strong
Greek term which is used in the Septuagint for the damming of a river. Paul refused to take money
from the Corinthian church and apparently he made this known publicly and often.

For "boasting" see full note at 2 Cor. 1:12.

SPECIAL TOPIC: BOASTING

verses.zh: 为甚么呢？是因我不爱你们吗？这有　神知道。
verses.en: Why? Because I do not love you? God knows I do![NOTE:1]
notes: Grk “God knows!” The words “I do” are supplied for clarity. Direct objects were often omitted in Greek when clear from the context.

verses.zh: 我现在所做的，后来还要做，为要断绝那些寻机会人的机会，使他们在所夸的事上也不过与我们一样。
verses.en: And what I am doing I will continue to do, so that I may eliminate any opportunity for those who want a chance to be regarded as our equals[NOTE:1] in the things they boast about.
notes: Grk “an opportunity, so that they may be found just like us.”
verses.commentary:
11:12 Paul knew his opponents. He tried to remove every opportunity for their attacks. He
limited his freedom and rights to protect and expand the gospel (cf. Rom. 14:1-15:13; 1 Cor. 9:19-23).
I am always impressed with Paul's comment in 1 Cor. 9:19-23!

verses.zh: 那等人是假使徒，行事诡诈，装作基督使徒的模样。
verses.en: For such people are false apostles, deceitful[NOTE:1] workers, disguising themselves[NOTE:2] as apostles of Christ.
notes: Or “dishonest.”
Or “workers, masquerading.”
verses.commentary:
11:13 "For such men are false apostles" These out-of-town religious leaders, possibly from
Jerusalem, claimed authority. Paul calls them pseudo-apostles and pseudo-brothers (cf. 2 Cor. 11:26).

SPECIAL TOPIC: APOSTASY

▣ "deceitful workers" This word is from the NOUN which meant "fishing bait."
They tried to catch the Corinthian believers for their own purposes and to further their reputations.

▣ "disguising themselves as apostles of Christ" These were not sincere Christians who were
misled. These were spiritually lost men (cf. 2 Cor. 11:14) attempting to divide the church of God
(cf. 1 Cor. 3:10-15). They were wolves in sheep's clothing (cf. Matthew 7; Acts 20:29; 2 Pet. 2:1-22;
Jude vv. 3-16).

The term "disguising" (i.e., metaschēmatizō) is used in 2 Cor. 11:13,14,15.
It speaks of the outward changing form of something or someone (cf. Phil. 3:21). These (i.e., false
teachers and Satan) appear to be what they are not!

SPECIAL TOPIC: FALSE TEACHERS

verses.zh: 这也不足为怪，因为连撒但也装作光明的天使。
verses.en: And no wonder, for even Satan disguises himself[NOTE:1] as an angel of light.
notes: Or “Satan himself masquerades.”
verses.commentary:
11:14 "for even Satan disguises himself as an angel of light" This is an obvious truth, but
is nowhere else in the Bible stated in these terms. This may be from rabbinical traditions about
Genesis 3 (cf. DSS cave 1, Manual of Discipline 3:20,24). Satan's major trick is masquerading
as truth (cf. Genesis 3). Evil always tries to mimic or counterfeit the good. False teachers always
come from inside the church (cf. 2 Pet. 2; 1 John 2:18-19; Jude).

SPECIAL TOPIC: PERSONAL EVIL

SPECIAL TOPIC: SATAN

verses.zh: 所以他的差役，若装作仁义的差役，也不算希奇。他们的结局必然照着他们的行为。
verses.en: Therefore it is not surprising his servants also disguise themselves[NOTE:1] as servants of righteousness, whose end will correspond to their actions.[NOTE:2]
notes: Or “also masquerade.”
Or “their works.”
verses.commentary:
11:15 "if" This is a FIRST CLASS CONDITIONAL SENTENCE. There were Satanically
inspired false teachers within the house churches at Corinth.

They are with us today!

▣ "servants of righteousness" Paul does not use "righteousness" often in the sense he
uses it here. Here it has the connotation of "goodness" or "rightness" (cf. Matt. 6:1), but not
in the theological sense of justification by grace through faith (cf. Rom. 3:21-23; Eph. 2:8-9).

SPECIAL TOPIC: RIGHTEOUSNESS

▣ "whose end will be according to their deeds" This seems to be an allusion to Prov. 24:12.
It is also the basic truth of the Bible. See full note at 2 Cor. 5:10 and a full list of parallel passages at Gal. 6:7.

verses.zh: 我再说，人不可把我看作愚妄的。纵然如此，也要把我当作愚妄人接纳，叫我可以略略自夸。
verses.en: I say again, let no one think that I am a fool.[NOTE:1] But if you do, then at least accept me as a fool, so that I too may boast a little.
notes: Or “am foolish.”
verses.commentary:
11:16 "let no one think me foolish. . .so that I also may boast a little" Paul was not comfortable
with personal boasting (cf. 2 Cor. 11:1,17). The false teachers had forced him to use their methods
(i.e., the literary style of chapters 10-13 reflects the characteristics of Hellenistic rhetorical forms).

For "foolish" see
SPECIAL TOPIC: FOOLISH PEOPLE

For "boast" see
SPECIAL TOPIC: BOASTING

▣ "if" This is an incomplete FIRST CLASS CONDITIONAL SENTENCE (i.e.,
no VERB). These Corinthian believers were surprised at Paul's letter.

SPECIAL TOPIC: GREEK GRAMMATICAL TERMS, VII.

verses.zh: 我说的话不是奉主命说的，乃是像愚妄人放胆自夸；
verses.en: What I am saying with this boastful confidence[NOTE:1] I do not say the way the Lord would.[NOTE:2] Instead it is, as it were, foolishness.
notes: Grk “with this confidence of boasting.” The genitive καυχήσεως (kauchēseōs) has been translated as an attributive genitive (the noun in the genitive functions as an adjective of the noun modified).
Or “say with the Lord’s authority.”
verses.commentary:
11:17 Paul alluded to Jesus' life and attitude in 2 Cor. 10:1 (i.e., by the meekness and
gentleness of Christ), but when it came to boasting or human comparisons, Paul must admit there
is no precedent in Jesus.

verses.zh: 既有好些人凭着血气自夸，我也要自夸了。
verses.en: Since many[NOTE:1] are boasting according to human standards,[NOTE:2] I too will boast.
notes: Many is a reference to Paul’s opponents.
Grk “according to the flesh.”
verses.commentary:
11:18 "Since many boast according to the flesh, I will boast also" This is the major focus of
chapters 10-13. The false teachers had attacked Paul and his gospel by comparing his heritage and
spiritual giftedness with theirs (cf. 2 Cor. 11:8). Paul was distressed that the church had listened
to them and had been swayed by their arguments. Therefore, he decided to get down on their level for the
purpose of winning this church back to confidence in his leadership and thereby renewed confidence in his gospel.

verses.zh: 你们既是精明人，就能甘心忍耐愚妄人。
verses.en: For since you are so wise, you put up with[NOTE:1] fools gladly.
notes: Or “you tolerate.”
verses.commentary:
11:19-20 This is biting sarcasm directed to the Corinthian church. Everything the false
teachers accused Paul of they practiced and a portion of the church positively responded to them!

▣ "tolerate" See note at 2 Cor. 11:4.

verses.zh: 假若有人强你们作奴仆，或侵吞你们，或掳掠你们，或侮慢你们，或打你们的脸，你们都能忍耐他。
verses.en: For you put up with[NOTE:1] it if someone makes slaves of you, if someone exploits you, if someone takes advantage of you, if someone behaves arrogantly[NOTE:2] toward you, if someone strikes you in the face.
notes: Or “you tolerate.”
verses.commentary:
11:20 "if anyone enslaves you" This starts a series of five FIRST CLASS CONDITIONAL
SENTENCES. This VERB (i.e., katadouloō) is only used here and
in Gal. 2:4 where it refers to the Judaizers. The Judaizers asserted that one had to become a full
Jew before one could become a Christian. How these false teachers relate to the Judaizers is uncertain.
The exact rules or rituals which the false teachers at Corinth put forth as necessary for salvation
are also uncertain (note the same issue addressed by Paul in Col. 2:16-23).

SPECIAL TOPIC: JUDAIZERS

▣ "if anyone devours you" Paul used this VERB only twice, here and
in Gal. 5:15, which also describes a church in conflict with false teachers.

NASB, NRSV, TEV
"takes advantage of you"

NKJV, Peshitta
"takes from you"

NJB
"keep you under his orders"

This is the common VERB lambanō, but with a figurative
extension of the literal sense of "to take hold of." Here it is to manipulate for personal advantage.

NASB, NKJV, Peshitta
"exalts himself"

NRSV
"puts on airs"

TEV
"look down on you"

NJB
"sets himself above you"

Paul used this same term in 2 Cor. 10:5 to describe the arrogance of the false
teachers' arguments and speculations. This term is simply the word "to lift up" (cf. 1 Tim. 2:8). But,
in 1 Corinthians it has negative connotations of human pride and arrogance.

▣ "hits you in the face" Paul's words drip with sarcasm (cf. 2 Cor. 11:21). He was
so gentle and meek (cf. 2 Cor. 10:1) with them, but they rejected him; the false teachers were
so selfish and manipulative, but parts of the church loved them.

verses.zh: 我说这话是羞辱自己，好像我们从前是软弱的。然而，人在何事上勇敢，（我说句愚妄话，）我也勇敢。
verses.en: (To my disgrace[NOTE:1] I must say that we were too weak for that!)[NOTE:2] But whatever anyone else dares to boast about[NOTE:3] (I am speaking foolishly), I also dare to boast about the same thing.[NOTE:4]
notes: Or “my shame.”

It seems best, in context, to see the statement we were too weak for that as a parenthetical and ironic comment by Paul on his physical condition (weakness or sickness) while he was with the Corinthians (cf. 2 Cor 12:7-10; Gal 4:15).

The words “to boast about” are not in the Greek text, but are implied. Direct objects were often omitted in Greek when clear from the context, and this phrase serves as the direct object of the preceding verb.

Grk “I also dare”; the words “to boast about the same thing” are not in the Greek text, but are implied. Direct objects were often omitted in Greek when clear from the context, and this phrase serves as the direct object of the preceding verb.
verses.commentary:
11:21 "to my shame" This is literally "according to dishonor." Paul felt that his
meekness and gentleness had been misunderstood and taken advantage of by the false teachers. This
may be another example of sarcasm.

▣ "weak" See

verses.zh: 他们是希伯来人吗？我也是。他们是以色列人吗？我也是。他们是亚伯拉罕的后裔吗？我也是。
verses.en: Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they descendants of Abraham? So am I.
verses.commentary:
11:22 "Are they Hebrews? So am I" This is the first of four rhetorical questions. "Hebrews"
idiomatically referred to the ability to speak Aramaic (cf. Acts 6:1), but with the implication of
true racial identity. This is another evidence that this group of false teachers had a Palestinian/Judaistic
origin.

This "so am I" (i.e., kagō) is repeated three times in 2 Cor. 11:22.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW PEOPLE

▣ "Are they Israelites? So am I" Apparently they were bragging that they were part of the
OT covenant people of God (cf. Phil. 3:5; John 8:31-59).

verses.zh: 他们是基督的仆人吗？（我说句狂话，）我更是。我比他们多受劳苦，多下监牢，受鞭打是过重的，冒死是屡次有的。
verses.en: Are they servants of Christ? (I am talking like I am out of my mind!) I am even more so: with much greater labors, with far more imprisonments, with more severe beatings, facing death many times.
verses.commentary:
11:23 "Are they servants of Christ?" Paul is not asserting here that they are Christians. He
is simply asserting, for the sake of argument, that he has the same spiritual credentials that they
are bragging about. They even claimed a spiritual superiority to Paul.

▣ "I more so" Paul had a series of comparisons with en.

- in far more labors, 2 Cor. 11:23

- in far more imprisonments, 2 Cor. 11:23

- in stripes above measure, 2 Cor. 11:23

- in danger of death often, 2 Cor. 11:23

- beaten with thirty nine lashes (5 times), 2 Cor. 11:24

- beaten with rods (3 times), 2 Cor. 11:25

- stoned (once), 2 Cor. 11:25

- shipwrecked (3 times), 2 Cor. 11:25

Some of these are recorded in Acts, but not most of them. In reality we know so little
of the first century church. Paul had paid a high price to speak the gospel (cf. 2 Cor. 4:7-12; 6:3-10!

verses.zh: 被犹太人鞭打五次，每次四十减去一下；
verses.en: Five times I received from the Jews forty lashes less one.[NOTE:1]
notes: Grk “forty less one”; this was a standard sentence. “Lashes” is supplied to clarify for the modern reader what is meant.
verses.commentary:
11:24 "I received from the Jews thirty-nine lashes" This refers to punishment administered
by Synagogue courts (cf. Deut. 25:1-3). The strokes were probably given with a rod (cf. Exod. 21:20;
Prov. 10:13; 19:29; 26:3) and given in public. This type of punishment was known and practiced in Assyria
and Egypt. It was also practiced in Israel (cf. Isa. 50:6; Jer. 20:2; 37:15).

The rabbis later codified that it had to be one less than forty strokes (i.e., the maximum
number, cf Josephus, Antiq. 4:8:21,23). They specified that so many hits be done on the back
and on the front, left and right shoulders (cf. Maccoth 3:10ff).

verses.zh: 被棍打了三次；被石头打了一次；遇着船坏三次，一昼一夜在深海里。
verses.en: Three times I was beaten with a rod.[NOTE:1] Once I received a stoning.[NOTE:2] Three times I suffered shipwreck. A night and a day I spent adrift in the open sea.
notes: Beaten with a rod refers to the Roman punishment of admonitio according to BDAG 902 s.v. ῥαβδίζω. Acts 16:22 describes one of these occasions in Philippi; in this case it was administered by the city magistrates, who had wide powers in a military colony.
Received a stoning. See Acts 14:19, where this incident is described.
verses.commentary:
11:25 "beaten with rods" This refers to a type of Roman judicial punishment (i.e., verberatio),
probably administered by a city court (cf. Acts 16:22-40; 1 Cor. 4:21) publicly.

▣ "once I was stoned" In Acts 14:19 his attackers stoned him and thought he was dead! This
may be the incident.

SPECIAL TOPIC: STONE TO DEATH

▣ "three times I was shipwrecked" This shows how limited the history of Acts truly is.
Paul's shipwreck recorded in Acts happened after this point in history. Acts is not a complete history,
but a theological account of the gospel moving from Palestine to Rome, from Jews to Gentiles.

verses.zh: 又屡次行远路，遭江河的危险、盗贼的危险、同族的危险、外邦人的危险、城里的危险、旷野的危险、海中的危险、假弟兄的危险。
verses.en: I have been on journeys many times, in dangers from rivers, in dangers from robbers,[NOTE:1] in dangers from my own countrymen, in dangers from Gentiles, in dangers in the city, in dangers in the wilderness,[NOTE:2] in dangers at sea, in dangers from false brothers,
notes: Or “bandits.” The word normally refers more to highwaymen (“robbers”) but can also refer to insurrectionists or revolutionaries (“bandits”).
Or “desert.”

Grk “in cold and nakedness.” Paul does not mean complete nakedness, however, which would have been repugnant to a Jew; he refers instead to the lack of sufficient clothing, especially in cold weather. A related word is used to 1 Cor 4:11, also in combination with experiencing hunger and thirst.
verses.commentary:
11:27 "I have been" Paul starts another list using the DATIVE/LOCATIVE.

- in labor

- in hardship

- in sleepless nights

- in hunger

- in thirst

- in fastings many times (lit. "often without food")

- in cold

- in nakedness (lit. "in exposure")

All of us who claim to be servants of the gospel should quit whining!

verses.zh: 除了这外面的事，还有为众教会挂心的事，天天压在我身上。
verses.en: Apart from other things,[NOTE:1] there is the daily pressure on me of my anxious concern[NOTE:2] for all the churches.
notes: Apart from other things. Paul refers here either (1) to the external sufferings just mentioned, or (2) he refers to other things he has left unmentioned.
“Anxious concern,” so translated in L&N 25.224.
verses.commentary:
11:28 Another thing which caused daily pain for Paul was the psychological/spiritual worry
for the health and effectiveness of the churches-possibly this was the worst pain of all!

verses.zh: 有谁软弱，我不软弱呢？有谁跌倒，我不焦急呢？

notes: Or “who is caused to stumble.”

11:29 "Who is weak without my being weak" Verse 29 has two rhetorical questions. When Paul

verses.zh: 在大马士革的亚哩达王手下的提督把守大马士革城，要捉拿我，
verses.en: In Damascus, the governor[NOTE:1] under King Aretas was guarding the city of Damascus[NOTE:2] in order to arrest[NOTE:3] me,
notes: Grk “ethnarch.”sn The governor was an official called an “ethnarch” who was appointed to rule on behalf of a king over a certain region.
Grk “the city of the Damascenes.”
Or “to seize,” “to catch.”
verses.commentary:
11:32-33 "In Damascus the ethnarch under Aretas" Some say this is anticlimactic, but this
was apparently the most embarrassing (i.e., weakest) moment of Paul's life. It could refer to
another charge of the false teachers. King Aretas (i.e., Harethath) was king of the Nabatean
empire from 9 B.C. to A.D. 40. He was the father-in-law of Herod
Antipas. The term "Aretas" is like the term "Pharaoh," a title for all of the Nabatean kings who
ruled in Petra. The "ethnarch" would have been Aretus' official representative in Damascus. The
account in Acts 9:23-25 is somewhat different; possibly the false teachers used this incident to
attack Paul's character.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

- 2 Corinthians 10-13 form a literary unit. In this section that is so different from
the previous chapters in 2 Corinthians, Paul defends himself against the attacks
of false teachers, probably in the house churches in Corinth. They had made Paul
himself the object of ridicule in their attempt to discredit his gospel.

- Paul answers the charges of his critics in chapter 2 Cor. 11:4,8,12-15,18-20.

- Paul uses irony and sarcasm to jog the memory of the Corinthian Christians
concerning his ministry (cf. 2 Cor. 11:5, 7, 19, 20, 21).
